The coronavirus will weigh on U.S. activity in the near term and heighten downside risks, but the FOMC’s rapid move to the effective lower bound, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and MBS, and expanded liquidity facilities are consistent with the literature showing countercyclical monetary policy can dampen fluctuations and support aggregate spending when inflation pressures are muted. Credit-channel evidence indicates such actions lower the external finance premium and help prevent deterioration of firm balance sheets—thereby cushioning business fixed investment and employment (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch 1996a; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist 1994). Dollar swap lines and repo operations also address global and domestic funding stress, aligning with research on imperfect information and credit markets during shocks. With market-based inflation compensation falling but longer-term expectations little changed, the policy stance supports price stability and maximum employment while avoiding the credibility mistakes of the 1970s. Net assessment: negative near-term outlook, partially offset by policy backstops.
